title: FBI Section 702 queries included people arrested at George Floyd protests
description_medium: A Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board report later documented that FBI personnel queried Section 702 databases for information about people arrested in connection with the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests. One incident involved 141 queries between June 3 and June 5, 2020. Section 702 collects foreign intelligence; searches using U.S. persons’ identifiers can retrieve communications already held in that database. The episode raised oversight concerns about the FBI’s use of the surveillance system.
description_long: In June 2020, FBI personnel conducted searches of data collected under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act using identifiers associated with people arrested during protests after George Floyd’s killing. A later report by the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board described an incident from June 3 to June 5 in which agents ran 141 queries connected to individuals arrested during Black Lives Matter demonstrations. Section 702 authorizes collection of communications involving foreign targets abroad, but the resulting database can include communications of Americans. FBI searches of that data using U.S. persons’ identifiers are subject to query rules and oversight. The board’s review raised concerns about whether searches had a sufficient factual basis and whether safeguards were followed. This episode formed part of broader scrutiny of FBI querying practices and the balance between intelligence gathering and Americans’ privacy. It involved searching an existing intelligence database; it did not mean the FBI intercepted every arrestee’s phone or email directly.
evidence_notes: PCLOB report documents the 141 queries June 3–5, 2020. Washington Post reports that people arrested at protests were among those whose identifiers were searched. The queries searched Section 702-acquired data, not direct collection from every arrestee.
corrected_wording: Specified that this refers to queries of Section 702-acquired databases, not direct interception of protesters’ personal accounts; removed unsupported declaration of illegality.

title: Ivana Trump described feeling violated after 1990 marital encounter
description_medium: During the Trumps’ 1990 divorce proceedings, Ivana Trump described an encounter after scalp surgery and used the word “rape” in an account published in a 1993 biography. Donald Trump denied the allegation. Ivana later said she did not intend the word in a literal or criminal sense, while maintaining that she had felt violated; in 2015, she called the story “without merit.” The allegation was never adjudicated in court.
description_long: Donald and Ivana Trump’s divorce proceedings in 1990 included a deposition in which Ivana described a violent sexual encounter after she had undergone scalp-reduction surgery. Journalist Harry Hurt III recounted the account in his 1993 biography of Donald Trump, quoting Ivana as using the word “rape.” Donald Trump denied that the encounter happened as described. Ivana’s lawyer later said she had used the word without intending a literal or criminal accusation, and Ivana said she had felt violated. When the story resurfaced during the 2015 presidential campaign, she called the account “without merit” and said she had a great relationship with her former husband. The differing statements have shaped public discussion of the allegation, but no court made a finding about it and Trump was not charged. The account is best understood as a serious allegation followed by clarification and denial, rather than an established criminal conviction or adjudicated fact.
evidence_notes: The New Yorker recounts the deposition and 1993 biography; Washington Post documents Ivana Trump’s later clarification, denial context, and 2015 statement. No adjudication established the allegation.
corrected_wording: Reframed the title and description as a reported allegation with subsequent clarification and denial; removed unsupported claims of systematic abuse and suppression.

title: Senate Intelligence Committee releases final report on Russia’s 2016 election interference
description_medium: On August 18, 2020, the bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee released the fifth and final volume of its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election. The report detailed counterintelligence risks arising from contacts between Russian-linked figures and people in Donald Trump’s campaign, including Paul Manafort’s sharing of internal campaign information with Konstantin Kilimnik. Its findings documented contacts and vulnerabilities; the headline’s claim that the committee found Trump won by “colluding” with Russia overstates the report.
description_long: On August 18, 2020, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released the fifth and final volume of its bipartisan investigation into Russian efforts to influence the 2016 U.S. election. The report examined counterintelligence threats and vulnerabilities involving the Trump campaign. It described contacts between campaign figures and people connected to Russia, including the June 2016 Trump Tower meeting, and found that campaign chairman Paul Manafort shared internal campaign polling information with Konstantin Kilimnik, whom the committee assessed had ties to Russian intelligence. The report also scrutinized how campaign associates responded to Russian offers and how they handled information about those contacts. The committee’s findings were serious and raised concerns about opportunities for Russian influence and access. They did not amount to a finding that Trump and his campaign conspired with Russia to win the election, as the supplied headline asserts. The report was a congressional counterintelligence investigation, not a criminal verdict, and its release renewed debate about the extent and significance of the campaign’s Russia contacts.
evidence_notes: Senate Committee announcement and Volume V support report date, scope, findings on Manafort/Kilimnik, and campaign contacts. The committee did not conclude that Trump won by colluding with Russia.
corrected_wording: Removed the unsupported assertion that Republicans agreed Trump won by collusion; stated the documented findings and their scope.

title: Trump Tower construction intersected with New York’s mob-influenced concrete industry
description_medium: Donald Trump’s Trump Tower project relied on concrete supplied through New York’s construction industry, where organized-crime figures had influence over contractors and unions. The Washington Post reported that Teamsters Local 282 leader John Cody was a labor racketeer and that Trump was questioned about his relationship with Cody, who allegedly sought an apartment in exchange for keeping the project on track. The supplied claim that workers were threatened with knives on Trump’s behalf is not established by the sources cited here.
description_long: Construction of Trump Tower in Manhattan took place in a period when organized-crime figures exerted influence over parts of New York’s concrete and construction industries. The Washington Post reported that Teamsters Local 282 leader John Cody controlled workers who delivered concrete and had been described in congressional records as a significant labor racketeer. Federal investigators questioned Donald Trump in 1980 about his relationship with Cody. According to the reporting, Cody had allegedly promised to keep the project moving in exchange for an apartment in the building. Other reporting documented that concrete for Trump projects came from companies owned by leaders of New York crime families. Those facts describe the project’s reliance on a labor and supply network under scrutiny for corruption and racketeering. The supplied account goes further, alleging that mob enforcers threatened workers with knives at Trump’s direction and that Trump knowingly used violence to suppress unions. Those specific claims are not established by the sources cited for this entry, and should not be presented as proven conduct. The documented record supports describing the industry context and reported relationship, with that distinction kept clear.
evidence_notes: WP reports Cody, the investigators’ questioning, and the alleged apartment arrangement; New Yorker outlines mob influence over construction and unions. The knife threats and Trump’s knowing participation in violence are not substantiated here.
corrected_wording: Limited account to documented labor-industry context and reported Cody relationship; excluded unsupported violence, criminal participation, and legal conclusions.
exact_blocker: The packet’s specific allegation that workers were threatened with knives on Trump’s behalf, and the claim Trump knowingly participated in violence to suppress unions, cannot be tied to a reliable event-specific source in the supplied references.

title: Trump says Pentagon leaders favor wars to please defense contractors
description_medium: At a September 7, 2020, White House Labor Day news conference, President Donald Trump accused senior Pentagon leaders of favoring continued wars to keep defense contractors happy. He contrasted the military leadership with rank-and-file service members, whom he said supported him, and again denied reports that he had disparaged fallen troops as “losers” and “suckers.” The remarks came during a period of tension between Trump and military leaders over U.S. deployments and his use of troops in domestic law enforcement.
description_long: President Donald Trump held a Labor Day news conference at the White House on September 7, 2020, during the presidential campaign and amid continuing controversy over reports that he had called fallen U.S. service members “losers” and “suckers.” At the briefing, Trump denied the reported comments and called the story a hoax. He also said senior Pentagon officials were unhappy with him because he wanted to end wars, and accused them of favoring continued conflict to keep defense contractors “happy.” Trump said rank-and-file military personnel supported him even though top leaders did not. His remarks followed earlier tension with defense officials over proposals to withdraw U.S. forces from Afghanistan and Germany and his threat to invoke the Insurrection Act during protests. The conference captured a public dispute between the commander in chief and senior military leadership over war policy and the military’s role. The remarks sharpened an already strained relationship between the White House and senior military leaders over U.S. deployments and the military’s role in domestic affairs.
evidence_notes: The archived transcript and contemporaneous reporting document the remarks and denial. The accusation that leaders sought wars to benefit contractors is Trump’s claim, not an established motive. Reports of the earlier comments about fallen troops were attributed and disputed.
corrected_wording: Replaced evaluative title with the specific statement made at the press conference; attributed motive claims to Trump.

title: Mary Trump sues Donald Trump and siblings, alleging inheritance fraud
description_medium: On September 24, 2020, Mary L. Trump sued Donald Trump, Maryanne Trump Barry, and the estate of Robert Trump in New York, alleging that they had misrepresented the value of her inherited interests in the family real-estate business and deprived her of millions of dollars. The defendants denied wrongdoing. The filing stated allegations, not findings by a court; a judge dismissed the suit in 2022, ruling that a 2001 settlement released Mary Trump’s claims.
description_long: Mary L. Trump filed a civil lawsuit in New York on September 24, 2020, accusing her uncle Donald Trump, her aunt Maryanne Trump Barry, and the estate of her uncle Robert Trump of fraud related to her inheritance from the family real-estate business. Her complaint said she and her brother inherited interests after their father, Fred Trump Jr., died, and alleged that the defendants misrepresented the value of those interests and pressured her to surrender them in a 2001 estate settlement. The suit sought damages and described a long-running dispute over the family fortune. The defendants denied the accusations. In November 2022, a New York judge dismissed the case, finding that the settlement Mary Trump had signed released her claims, including claims she later framed as fraud. The dismissal ended the case without a trial of the underlying allegations. The underlying allegations remain disputed.
evidence_notes: Complaint and contemporaneous reporting describe allegations; New York court opinion and Reuters coverage support November 2022 dismissal based on the 2001 settlement and release.
corrected_wording: Added filing date, principal allegations, and disposition; retained allegation language and avoided presenting claims as proven.

title: EPA revises pesticide application exclusion zones in 2020 rule
description_medium: On October 30, 2020, the Trump-era Environmental Protection Agency finalized revisions to the Application Exclusion Zone requirements in the Agricultural Worker Protection Standard. The rule limited the exclusion zone’s enforceability to the boundaries of the agricultural establishment, simplified the distance to 25 feet for many ground-sprayed applications, and retained a 100-foot zone for certain other methods. Farmworker advocates said the changes weakened protections; EPA described them as clarifying and simplifying the rules.
description_long: The Environmental Protection Agency finalized revisions to its pesticide Application Exclusion Zone requirements on October 30, 2020. The zone is an area around pesticide application equipment where workers and other people must be kept away while spraying is underway. Under the 2015 Worker Protection Standard, zones could extend beyond a farm’s boundaries and varied by application method. The Trump-era revision limited the zone’s enforcement to the agricultural establishment, simplified it to 25 feet for many ground applications sprayed from more than 12 inches above the ground, and retained a 100-foot zone for aerial, air-blast, fumigant, mist, and fog applications. The rule also changed how employers could resume spraying after people entered a zone and allowed an owner’s immediate family to remain in closed shelters during certain applications. EPA said the revisions would clarify and simplify compliance while maintaining worker protections. Farmworker and environmental advocates argued that limiting the zone’s reach and reducing its size for some applications could leave workers and nearby residents more exposed to pesticide drift. EPA later reversed parts of the 2020 revisions.
evidence_notes: EPA’s 2020 final rule and 2024 restoration notice support the specific changes and later reversal. Describing increased exposure as a possible effect reflects critics’ position rather than a quantified exposure outcome.
corrected_wording: Specified the actual AEZ amendments and date; replaced unsupported categorical claim of increased exposure with attributed concerns and the rule’s detailed effects.

title: Trump rejects election result and vows legal challenges after Biden is projected winner
description_medium: On November 7, 2020, after news organizations projected Joe Biden as the winner of the presidential election, Donald Trump issued a statement refusing to concede and promising legal action. He argued that counting was unfinished and alleged that his campaign had valid challenges in several states. The statement did not provide evidence for widespread fraud, and election officials later certified the results; courts rejected challenges that sought to change the outcome.
description_long: On November 7, 2020, news organizations projected that Joe Biden had won the presidential election after results in Pennsylvania put him ahead in the Electoral College. Donald Trump did not concede. In a statement released by his campaign, he said that Biden had not been certified as the winner of any state, claimed the election was “far from over,” and said his campaign would begin pursuing legal challenges the following week. Trump’s statement also alleged that the campaign had legitimate challenges in contested states. At the time, election officials were still completing certification procedures, but those procedures did not alter the result. Trump and his allies filed lawsuits challenging vote counts and election rules in multiple states; courts dismissed or rejected challenges that sought to overturn the outcome. The refusal to concede marked the start of an extended effort to contest Biden’s victory, which was later certified by Congress on January 6, 2021. The dispute continued through the transition, as states certified their results and Congress counted the electoral votes on January 6, 2021.
evidence_notes: PBS reproduces Trump’s full statement; AP and contemporaneous reporting document Biden’s projection, refusal to concede, and subsequent court challenges. Use certification as distinct from the media projection.
corrected_wording: Kept the refusal and legal-threat event, corrected the inaccurate “first president since 1992” claim, and distinguished projection, certification, and unsupported fraud allegations.
